text: 3 Distance Encoding and Its Power
3.1 Distance Encoding

Suppose we are to learn the structural representation of the target node set [MATH S] . Intuitively, we propose DE to encode certain distance from [MATH S] to a node [MATH u] . Rigorously, we define DE as follows.

Given a target set of nodes [MATH S\in 2^{V}\backslash\emptyset] of [MATH G] with the adjacency matrix [MATH A] , denote distance encoding as a function [MATH \zeta(\cdot|S,A):V\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{k}] . [MATH \zeta] should also be permutation invariant, i.e., [MATH \zeta(u|S,A)=\zeta(\pi(u)|\pi(S),\pi(A))] for all [MATH u\in V] and [MATH \pi\in\Pi_{n}] . We denote DEs w.r.t. the size of [MATH S] and call them as DE- [MATH p] if [MATH |S|=p] .

Later we use [MATH \zeta(u|S)] for brevity where [MATH A] could be inferred from the context. For simplicity, we choose DE as a set aggregation (e.g., the sum-pooling) of DEs between nodes [MATH u,\,v] where [MATH v\in S] :
[MATH \displaystyle\zeta(u|S)=\text{AGG}(\{\zeta(u|v)|v\in S\})] (1)

More complicated DE may be used while this simple design can be efficiently implemented and achieves good empirical performance. Then, the problem reduces to choosing a proper [MATH \zeta(u|v)] . Again for simplicity, we consider the following class of functions that is based on the mapping of a list of landing probabilities of random walks from [MATH v] to [MATH u] over the graph, i.e.,
[MATH \displaystyle\zeta(u|v)=f_{3}(\ell_{uv}),\;\ell_{uv}=((W)_{uv},(W^{2})_{uv},...,(W^{k})_{uv},...)] (2)

where [MATH W=AD^{-1}] is the random walk matrix, [MATH f_{3}] may be simply designed by some heuristics or be parameterized and learnt as a feed-forward neural network. In practice, a finite length of [MATH \ell_{vu}] , say 3,4, is enough. Note that (2) covers many important measures. First, setting [MATH f_{3}(\ell_{uv})] as the first non-zero position in [MATH \ell_{uv}] gives the shortest-path-distance (SPD) from [MATH v] to [MATH u] . We denote this specific choice as [MATH \zeta_{spd}(u|v)] . Second, one may choose generalized PageRank scores [34]:
[MATH \displaystyle\zeta_{gpr}(u|v)=\sum_{k\geq 1}\gamma_{k}(W^{k})_{uv}=(\sum_{k\geq 1}\gamma_{k}W^{k})_{uv},\quad\gamma_{k}\in\mathbb{R},\,\text{for all $k\in\mathbb{N}$ }.] (3)

Note that permutation invariance of DE is beneficial for inductive learning, which fundamentally differs from positional node embeddings such as node2vec [37] or one-hot node identifiers. In the rest of this work, we will show that DE improves the expressive power of GNNs in both theory and practice. In Section 3.2, we use DE as extra node features. We term this model as DEGNN, and theoretically demonstrate its expressive power. In the next subsection, we further use DE-1 to control the aggregation procedure of WLGNN. We term this model as DEAGNN and extend our theory there.
3.2 DEGNN — Distance Encodings as Node Features

DE can be used as extra node features. Specifically, we improve WLGNNs by setting [MATH h_{v}^{(0)}=\mathbf{A}_{vv}\oplus\zeta(v|S)] where [MATH \oplus] is the concatenation. We call the obtained model DEGNN. We similarly use DEGNN- [MATH p] to specify the case when [MATH |S|=p] . For simplicity, we give the following definition.
DEGNN is called proper if [MATH f_{1},f_{2}] , AGGs in the WLGNN (Fig. 1 (b)), and AGG in Eq. (1), [MATH f_{3}] in Eq. (2) are injective mappings as long as the input features are all countable.
We know that a proper DEGNN exists because of the universal approximation theorem of feed-forward networks (to construct [MATH f_{i}] , [MATH i\in\{1,2,3\}] ) and Deep Sets [38] (to construct AGGs).
3.2.1 The Expressive Power of DEGNN

Next, we demonstrate the power of DEGNN to distinguish structural representations. Recall that the fundamental limit of WLGNN is the 1-WL test for structural representation (Theorem 2.7). One important class of graphs that cannot be distinguished by the 1-WL test are regular graphs, although, in practice, node/edge attributes may help diminish such difficulty by breaking the symmetry. In theory, we may consider the most difficult case by assuming that no node/edge attributes are available. In the following, our main theorem shows that even in the most difficult case, DEGNN is able to distinguish two equal-sized node sets that are embedded in almost all [MATH r] -regular graphs. One example where DEGNN using [MATH \zeta_{spd}(\cdot)] (SPD) is shown in Fig. 1 (a): The blue nodes can be easily distinguished from the green or red nodes as SPD [MATH =3] may appear between two nodes when a blue node is the node set of interest, while all SPDs from other nodes to red and green nodes are less than 3. Actually, DEGNN-1 with SPD may also distinguish the red or green nodes by investigating its procedure in details (Fig. 3 in Appendix).

Given two equal-sized sets [MATH S^{(1)},S^{(2)}\subset V] , [MATH |S^{(1)}|=|S^{(2)}|] . Consider two tuples [MATH \mathcal{T}^{(1)}=(S^{(1)},\mathbf{A}^{(1)})] and [MATH \mathcal{T}^{(2)}=(S^{(2)},\mathbf{A}^{(2)})] in the most difficult setting where features [MATH \mathbf{A}^{(1)}] and [MATH \mathbf{A}^{(2)}] are only different in graph structures specified by [MATH A^{(1)}] and [MATH A^{(2)}] respectively. Suppose [MATH A^{(1)}] and [MATH A^{(2)}] are uniformly independently sampled from all r-regular graphs over [MATH V] where [MATH 3\leq r<(2\log n)^{1/2}] . Then, for some small constant [MATH \epsilon>0] , within [MATH L\leq\lceil(\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon)\frac{\log n}{\log(r-1)}\rceil] layers, there exists a proper DEGNN- [MATH p] using DEs [MATH \zeta(u|S^{(1)}),\,\zeta(u|S^{(2)})] for all [MATH u\in V] , such that with probability [MATH 1-o(n^{-1})] , the outputs [MATH \Gamma(\mathcal{T}^{(1)})\neq\Gamma(\mathcal{T}^{(2)})] . Specifically, [MATH f_{3}] can be simply chosen as SPD, i.e., [MATH \zeta(u|v)=\zeta_{spd}(u|v)] . The big-O notations here and later are w.r.t. [MATH n] .

In some cases, we are to learn representations of structures that lie in a single large graph, i.e., [MATH A^{(1)}=A^{(2)}] . Actually, there is no additional difficulty to extend the proof of Theorem 3.3 to this setting as long as [MATH A^{(1)}(=A^{(2)})] is uniformly sampled from all r-regular graphs and [MATH S^{(1)}\cap S^{(2)}=\emptyset] . The underlying intuition is that for large [MATH n] , the local subgraphs (within [MATH L] -hop neighbors) around two non-overlapping fixed sets [MATH S^{(1)},S^{(2)}] are almost independent. Simulation results to validate the single node case ( [MATH p=1] ) of Theorem 3.3 and Remark 3.1 are shown in Fig. 2 (a).

Theorem 3.3 focuses on node sets embedded in regular graphs. A natural question therefore arises: how about the power of DEs to distinguish non-isomorphic node sets embedded in irregular graphs that the 1-WL test (also WLGNN) may not distinguish. To any this question, note that there is some important connection between irregular graphs and regular graphs under the umbrella of the 1-WL test. Actually, the partition of nodes over irregular graphs according to their representations (colors) stably associated by the 1-WL test has equitable property [39]. Basically, suppose that the whole node set [MATH V] can be partitioned into several parts based on the representations (colors) of nodes, [MATH V=\cup_{i=1}^{c}V_{i}] , where for an arbitrary [MATH i] , nodes in [MATH V_{i}] share the same representations based on the 1-WL test. Then, the induced subgraph of the nodes in [MATH V_{i}] is a regular graph for all [MATH i] ’s. What’s more, for any [MATH i,j] , the number of nodes in [MATH V_{j}] that are neighbors of a certain node in [MATH V_{i}] is shared by all the nodes in [MATH V_{i}] , which again shows certain regularity. Theoretically, if we focus on the regular subgraph defined over each [MATH V_{i}] , we may further leverage DE defined over this subgraph to further distinguish the nodes in [MATH V_{i}] . In practice, we do not need to work on each subgraph individually and mostly the capability of DE indicated by Theorem 3.3 may still help with breaking such regularity.

Actually, the power of structural representations of small node sets can be used to further characterize the power of graph representation. Consider that we directly aggregate all the representations of nodes of a graph output by DEGNN-1 via set-pooling as the entire-graph representation, which is a common strategy adopted to learn graph representation via WLGNN-1 [14, 16, 23]. So how about the power of DEGNN-1 to represent graphs? To answer this question, suppose two [MATH n] -sized [MATH r] -regular graphs [MATH \mathbf{A}^{(1)}] and [MATH \mathbf{A}^{(2)}] satisfy the condition in Theorem 3.3. Then, by using a union bound, Theorem 3.3 indicates that for a node [MATH v\in V] , its representation [MATH \Gamma((v,\mathbf{A}^{(1)}))\not\in\{\Gamma((u,\mathbf{A}^{(2)}))|u\in V\}] with probability [MATH 1-no(n^{-1})=1-o(1)] . Therefore, these two graphs [MATH \mathbf{A}^{(1)}] and [MATH \mathbf{A}^{(2)}] can be distinguished via DEGNN-1 with high probability. We formally state this result in the following corollary.

Suppose two graphs are uniformly independently sampled from all [MATH n] -sized [MATH r] -regular graphs over [MATH V] where [MATH 3\leq r<(2\log n)^{1/2}] . Then, within [MATH L\leq\lceil(\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon)\frac{\log n}{\log(r-1)}\rceil] layers, DEGNN-1 can distinguish these two graphs with probability [MATH 1-o(1)] by being concatenated with injective set-pooling over all the representations of nodes.
3.2.2 The Limitation of DEGNN

Next, we show the limitation of DEGNN. We prove that over a subclass of regular graphs, distance regular graph (DRG), on which DE-1 is useless for structural representation. We provide the definition of DRG as follows while we refer interested readers to check more properties of DRGs in [35].

A distance regular graph is a regular graph such that for any two nodes [MATH v,u\in V] , the number of vertices [MATH w] s.t. SPD [MATH (w,v)=i] and SPD [MATH (w,u)=j] , only depends on [MATH i] , [MATH j] and SPD [MATH (v,u)] .

Shrikhande graph and [MATH 4\times 4] Rook’s graph are two non-isomorphic DRGs shown in Fig. 2 (b) (We temporarily ignore the nodes colors which will be discussed later). For simplicity, we only consider connected DRGs that can be characterized by arrays of integers termed intersection arrays.

The intersection array of a connected DRG with diameter [MATH \triangle] is an array of integers [MATH \{b_{0},b_{1},...,b_{\triangle-1};c_{1},c_{2},...,c_{\triangle}\}] such that for any node pair [MATH (u,v)\in V\times V] that satisfies SPD [MATH (v,u)=j] , [MATH b_{j}] is the number of nodes [MATH w] that are neighbors of [MATH v] and satisfy SPD [MATH (w,u)=j+1] , and [MATH c_{j}] is the number of nodes [MATH w] that are neighbors of [MATH v] and satisfy SPD [MATH (w,u)=j-1] .

It is not hard to show that the two DRGs in Fig. 2 (b) share the same intersecion array [MATH \{6,3;1,2\}] . The following theorem shows that over distance regular graphs, DEGNN-1 must distinguish structures with discriminatory node/edge attributes, which indicates the limitation of DE-1.

Given any two nodes [MATH v,u\in V] , consider two tuples [MATH \mathcal{T}_{1}=(v,\mathbf{A}^{(1)})] and [MATH \mathcal{T}_{2}=(u,\mathbf{A}^{(2)})] with graph structures [MATH A^{(1)}] and [MATH A^{(2)}] that correspond to two connected DRGs with a same intersection array. Then, DEGNN-1 must use discriminatory node/edge attributes to distinguish [MATH \mathcal{T}_{1}] and [MATH \mathcal{T}_{2}] .
Note Theorem 3.7 only works for node representations using DE-1. Therefore, DEGNN-1 may not associate distinguishable node representations in the two DRGs in Fig. 2 (b).

However, if we are to learn higher-order structural representations ( [MATH |S|\geq 2] ) with DE- [MATH p] ( [MATH p\geq 2] ), DEGNN-p may have even stronger representation power. We illustrate this point by considering structural representations of two node-pairs that form edges of the two DRGs respectively. Consider two node-pairs that correspond to two edges of these two graphs in Fig. 2 (b) respectively. Then, there exists a proper DEGNN-2 via using SPD as DE-2, whose outputs associate these two node-pairs with different representations. Moreover, by simply aggregating the obtained representations of all node-pairs into graph representations via a set-pooling, we may also distinguish these two graphs. Note that distinguishing the node-pairs of the two DRGs is really hard, because even the 2-WL test 11 1 We follow the terminology 2-WL test in [40], which refines representations of node-pairs iteratively and is proved to be more powerful than 1-WL test. This 2-WL test is termed 2-WL’ test in [41] or 2-FWL test in [30]. A brief introduction of higher-order WL tests can be found in Appendix G. will fail to distinguish any edges in the DRGs with a same intersection array and diameters exactly equal to 2 22 2 Actually, the 2-WL test may not distinguish edges in a special class of DRGs, termed strongly regular graphs (SRG) [40]. A connected SRG is a DRG with diameter constrained as 2 [42]..

It is interesting to generalize Theorem 3.3 to SRGs to demonstrate the power of DEGNN- [MATH p] ( [MATH p\geq 2] ). However, missing analytic-friendly random models for SRGs makes such generalization challenging.
4 Related Works

Recently, extensive effort has been taken to improve the structural representation power of WLGNN. From the theoretical perspective, most previous works only considered representations of entire graphs [27, 28, 29, 30, 25, 43, 44] while Srinivasan & Ribeiro initialized the investigation of structural representations of node sets [45] from the view of joint probabilistic distributions. Some works view GNNs as general approximators of invariant functions but the proposed models hold more theoretical implication than practical usage because of their dependence on polynomial [MATH (n)] -order tensors [28, 46, 47]. Ring-GNN [29] (or equivalently PPGN [30]), a relatively scalable model among them, was based on 3-order tensors and was proposed to achieve the expressive power of the 2-WL test (a brief introduction in Appendix G). However, Ring-GNN (PPGN) was proposed for entire-graph representations and cannot leverage the sparsity of the graph structure to be scalable enough to process large graphs [29, 30]. DEGNN still benefits from such sparsity and are also used to represent node sets of arbitrary sizes. Moreover, our models theoretically behave orthogonal to Ring-GNN, as DE-2 can distinguish some non-isomorphic node-pairs that Ring-GNN fails to distinguish because the power of Ring-GNN is limited by the 2-WL test (Fig. 2 (b)).

Some works with empirical success inspire the proposal of DE, though we are the first one to derive theoretical characterization and leverage our theory to better those models as a return. SEAL [9] predicts links by reading out the representations of ego-networks of node-pairs. Although SEAL leverages a specific DE-2, the representations of those ego-networks are extracted via complex SortPooling [23]. However, we argue against such complex operations as DE-2 yields all the benefit of representations of node-pairs, as demonstrated by our experiments. PGNN [10] uses SPDs between each node and some anchor nodes to encode distance between nodes. As those encodings are not permutation invariant, PGNN holds worse inductive/generalization capability than our models.

Quite a few works targeted at revising neighbor aggregation procedure of WLGNN and thus are related to the DEAGNN. However, none of them demystified their connection to DE or provided theoretical characterization. MixHop [48], PAGTN [31], MAT [17] essentially used [MATH \zeta_{spd}(u|v)] to change the way of aggregation (Eq. (4)) while GDC [32] and PowerGNN [49] used variants of [MATH \zeta_{gpr}(u|v)] . MixHop, GDC and PowerGNN are evaluated for node classification while PAGTN and MAT are evaluated for graph classification. GDC claims that the aggregation based on [MATH \zeta_{gpr}(u|v)] does not help link prediction. However, we are able to show its empirical success for link prediction, as the key point missed by GDC is using DEs as extra node attributes (Appendix F.3).
